Free response · work it on paper Question 1 of 5
  1. 1

    1. Where the new rule actually gets spent . Foundational, 11 points. Question 1 of 5.

    Foundational 11 pts

    Complex arithmetic is the algebra you already knew plus one substitution, and it is worth knowing exactly where that substitution enters and what else had to be established before an operation could be attempted at all. Take z=14−5iz = 14 - 5iz=14−5i and w=4+iw = 4 + iw=4+i through all four operations, then account for the machinery each one used.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Write z+wz + wz+w,   z−w\;z - wz−w,   zw\;zwzw and   zw\;\dfrac{z}{w}wz​ in standard form.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Expand (14−5x)(4+x)(14 - 5x)(4 + x)(14−5x)(4+x) as a polynomial in an ordinary letter xxx, and separately expand (14−5i)(4+i)(14 - 5i)(4 + i)(14−5i)(4+i) term by term. The two expansions agree for a while and then stop agreeing. Identify the exact term where they part company, and say what the rule i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1 does to it.

      Compare the two methods Say what each one costs you, and when you would reach for it. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Sort the four operations by the machinery each one needs: which rest on nothing but the commutative, associative and distributive laws, which also spend i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1, and which one could not be attempted at all until something had been PROVED. Name the fact that had to be proved and say what it guarantees. Then say what shape all four of the results in part A share, and decide whether that shape was forced or was a feature of these particular numbers.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 3 points

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 3

      Try all four operations on 14−5x14 - 5x14−5x and 4+x4 + x4+x instead, where xxx is nothing but a letter. Three of them hand back something of the same shape they started with and one of them does not, which is the first sorting. Then ask, separately, which of those three throws up a stray x2x^2x2 that has nowhere to go.

    2. Hint 2 of 3 · Part B

      Finish the letter version completely before looking at the other one, then set the two side by side and read them left to right. Stop at the first place where one of them can take a step the other cannot.

    3. Hint 3 of 3 · Part C

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    z+w=18−4iz + w = 18 - 4iz+w=18−4i,   z−w=10−6i\;z - w = 10 - 6iz−w=10−6i,   zw=61−6i\;zw = 61 - 6izw=61−6i, and   zw=3−2i\;\dfrac{z}{w} = 3 - 2iwz​=3−2i.

    • Any of the four may be written with the sign inside the imaginary slot, as in 18+(−4)i18 + (-4)i18+(−4)i; that is the same standard form
    • The quotient may be reached through 51−34i17\dfrac{51 - 34i}{17}1751−34i​, but a single fraction is not yet standard form, so both parts must end up divided

    Part B

    Both distributions produce the same four partial products, term for term. They part company only when the last one is simplified: −5x2-5x^2−5x2 can go no further, while −5i2-5i^2−5i2 becomes +5+5+5 and leaves the imaginary column for the real one, turning 56−6x−5x256 - 6x - 5x^256−6x−5x2 into 61−6i61 - 6i61−6i.

    Part C

    The demands are cumulative. Addition and subtraction use only the three laws; multiplication uses those and spends i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1; division spends it twice more and needs a theorem first: for w=c+di≠0w = c + di \neq 0w=c+di=0, w w‾=c2+d2w\,\overline{w} = c^2 + d^2ww=c2+d2 is a nonzero real. All four results have the form a+bia + bia+bi, which is closure, not luck.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Take the four operations in order, and finish each one before starting the next.

    Addition combines like terms, the real parts with the real parts and the imaginary parts with the imaginary parts:

    z+w=(14+4)+(−5+1) i=18−4i.z + w = (14 + 4) + (-5 + 1)\,i = 18 - 4i.z+w=(14+4)+(−5+1)i=18−4i.

    Subtraction is the same computation once the minus sign has been distributed through BOTH terms of www, which is where this operation is usually lost:

    z−w=14−5i−4−i=(14−4)+(−5−1) i=10−6i.z - w = 14 - 5i - 4 - i = (14 - 4) + (-5 - 1)\,i = 10 - 6i.z−w=14−5i−4−i=(14−4)+(−5−1)i=10−6i.

    Multiplication expands term by term, exactly as for two binomials, and only then is the new rule spent on the i2i^2i2:

    zw=56+14i−20i−5i2=56−6i+5=61−6i.zw = 56 + 14i - 20i - 5i^2 = 56 - 6i + 5 = 61 - 6i.zw=56+14i−20i−5i2=56−6i+5=61−6i.

    Division multiplies above and below by the conjugate of the denominator, 4−i4 - i4−i. That is multiplying by 111, so it changes the costume of the fraction and not its value:

    14−5i4+i=(14−5i)(4−i)(4+i)(4−i)=56−14i−20i+5i242+12.\frac{14 - 5i}{4 + i} = \frac{(14 - 5i)(4 - i)}{(4 + i)(4 - i)} = \frac{56 - 14i - 20i + 5i^2}{4^2 + 1^2}.4+i14−5i​=(4+i)(4−i)(14−5i)(4−i)​=42+1256−14i−20i+5i2​.

    The denominator is a conjugate product, so it is the real number 171717, and the numerator collects to 51−34i51 - 34i51−34i. Dividing each part by 171717 finishes the job:

    51−34i17=5117+−3417 i=3−2i.\frac{51 - 34i}{17} = \frac{51}{17} + \frac{-34}{17}\,i = 3 - 2i.1751−34i​=1751​+17−34​i=3−2i.

    A quotient is worth checking, because the check costs one multiplication:

    (3−2i)(4+i)=12+3i−8i−2i2=14−5i.(3 - 2i)(4 + i) = 12 + 3i - 8i - 2i^2 = 14 - 5i.(3−2i)(4+i)=12+3i−8i−2i2=14−5i.

    Part B

    Run both expansions the same way, distributing every term of the first factor across every term of the second, and do not simplify either one early.

    With an ordinary letter:

    (14−5x)(4+x)=56+14x−20x−5x2=56−6x−5x2.(14 - 5x)(4 + x) = 56 + 14x - 20x - 5x^2 = 56 - 6x - 5x^2.(14−5x)(4+x)=56+14x−20x−5x2=56−6x−5x2.

    With the imaginary unit, the four partial products are formed by the identical distribution:

    (14−5i)(4+i)=56+14i−20i−5i2.(14 - 5i)(4 + i) = 56 + 14i - 20i - 5i^2.(14−5i)(4+i)=56+14i−20i−5i2.

    Compare them term by term. The constant term 565656 matches, and the two middle terms 14x14x14x and −20x-20x−20x match 14i14i14i and −20i-20i−20i, collecting to −6x-6x−6x and −6i-6i−6i. Nothing new has happened yet, which is the point: the expansion itself knows nothing about iii.

    The fourth term is where they separate. In the polynomial, −5x2-5x^2−5x2 is a term of a kind the other two are not, so it stays where it is and the expression is finished. In the complex product, i2i^2i2 is not a new kind of thing at all, because the definition says what it equals:

    −5i2=−5(−1)=+5.-5i^2 = -5(-1) = +5.−5i2=−5(−1)=+5.

    That term therefore abandons the imaginary column and joins the real part, which is why the real part of the answer is 56+5=6156 + 5 = 6156+5=61 rather than 565656:

    56−6i+5=61−6i.56 - 6i + 5 = 61 - 6i.56−6i+5=61−6i.

    So the whole difference between multiplying complex numbers and multiplying binomials is one term and one substitution. Everything else was distribution, and the polynomial version had to stop at three terms while the complex version collapsed to two.

    Part C

    Sort by what each operation would break without.

    Addition and subtraction. Regrouping (14−5i)+(4+i)(14 - 5i) + (4 + i)(14−5i)+(4+i) into real terms and imaginary terms uses commutativity and associativity, and collecting −5i+i-5i + i−5i+i into (−5+1)i(-5 + 1)i(−5+1)i uses distributivity. That is the whole computation. The value of i2i^2i2 never comes up, because no two iii symbols are ever multiplied together.

    Multiplication. The expansion is again distributivity, four times over. Then one term contains i2i^2i2, and the definition is spent on it. So multiplication needs the three laws plus the one new fact, and nothing else.

    Division. This one cannot even start. Writing zw\frac{z}{w}wz​ is only meaningful if www has a reciprocal, and the recipe for producing one is to multiply above and below by w‾\overline{w}w, which is worth doing only because of a theorem proved in the lesson, for w=c+diw = c + diw=c+di with ccc and ddd real:

    w w‾=(c+di)(c−di)=c2+d2.w\,\overline{w} = (c + di)(c - di) = c^2 + d^2.ww=(c+di)(c−di)=c2+d2.

    That guarantees two things at once. The new denominator is REAL, so the last step is dividing each part of a complex number by a real number, an operation already understood. And it is NONZERO whenever w≠0w \neq 0w=0, since a sum of two real squares is zero only when both are, so the recipe never divides by 000 except when www itself is 000.

    Division does not escape the first two demands, it adds to them. The conjugate product above is itself a multiplication in which −d2i2-d^2i^2−d2i2 becomes +d2+d^2+d2, and the numerator (14−5i)(4−i)(14 - 5i)(4 - i)(14−5i)(4−i) is another ordinary complex multiplication, so the rule i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1 is spent twice more before the answer appears. The right way to read the sort is therefore cumulative rather than exclusive: addition and subtraction need the laws; multiplication needs the laws and the rule; division needs the laws, the rule, and a theorem before it can begin at all.

    The shape they share. Every one of 18−4i18 - 4i18−4i, 10−6i10 - 6i10−6i, 61−6i61 - 6i61−6i and 3−2i3 - 2i3−2i is a real number plus a real multiple of iii. That was forced. Addition and subtraction produce sums and differences of real numbers in the two slots; multiplication produces (ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i(ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)i, whose slots are built from real numbers by real arithmetic; and division ends with two real quotients over the same real denominator. Being closed under the four operations is what makes the complex numbers a place to do mathematics rather than a notation that occasionally escapes itself.

    In one line

    z+w=18−4iz + w = 18 - 4iz+w=18−4i, z−w=10−6iz - w = 10 - 6iz−w=10−6i, zw=61−6izw = 61 - 6izw=61−6i and zw=3−2i\dfrac{z}{w} = 3 - 2iwz​=3−2i. The letter expansion 56−6x−5x256 - 6x - 5x^256−6x−5x2 and the complex one produce the same four partial products and separate only when the last is simplified: −5i2-5i^2−5i2 becomes +5+5+5 and joins the real part, giving 61−6i61 - 6i61−6i. The three demands are cumulative: addition and subtraction use only the commutative, associative and distributive laws; multiplication uses those and spends i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1; division spends the rule twice more on top of that, in the numerator and in the conjugate product, and in addition needs the theorem that w w‾=c2+d2w\,\overline{w} = c^2 + d^2ww=c2+d2 is real and nonzero for w=c+di≠0w = c + di \neq 0w=c+di=0, which is what makes the denominator clearable. All four results have the form a+bia + bia+bi, because the system is closed under all four operations.

    Try a similar problem (Optional)

    Same idea, different numbers. Work it on paper, then check yourself the same way.

    Let z=1+8iz = 1 + 8iz=1+8i and w=2+iw = 2 + iw=2+i. Write z+wz + wz+w, z−wz - wz−w, zwzwzw and zw\dfrac{z}{w}wz​ in standard form, and say in one line which of the four computations used the rule i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1.

    The answer

    z+w=3+9iz + w = 3 + 9iz+w=3+9i, z−w=−1+7iz - w = -1 + 7iz−w=−1+7i, zw=−6+17izw = -6 + 17izw=−6+17i and zw=2+3i\dfrac{z}{w} = 2 + 3iwz​=2+3i. The rule i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1 was used in the product and in the quotient, and not in the sum or the difference.

    The two additive computations are collections:

    z+w=3+9i,z−w=(1−2)+(8−1) i=−1+7i.z + w = 3 + 9i, \qquad z - w = (1 - 2) + (8 - 1)\,i = -1 + 7i.z+w=3+9i,z−w=(1−2)+(8−1)i=−1+7i.

    The product expands, and the last term is where the rule is spent:

    zw=2+i+16i+8i2=2+17i−8=−6+17i.zw = 2 + i + 16i + 8i^2 = 2 + 17i - 8 = -6 + 17i.zw=2+i+16i+8i2=2+17i−8=−6+17i.

    The quotient multiplies above and below by 2−i2 - i2−i, and the denominator becomes 22+12=52^2 + 1^2 = 522+12=5:

    1+8i2+i=(1+8i)(2−i)5=2−i+16i−8i25=10+15i5=2+3i.\frac{1 + 8i}{2 + i} = \frac{(1 + 8i)(2 - i)}{5} = \frac{2 - i + 16i - 8i^2}{5} = \frac{10 + 15i}{5} = 2 + 3i.2+i1+8i​=5(1+8i)(2−i)​=52−i+16i−8i2​=510+15i​=2+3i.

    Only the product and the quotient used i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1: the quotient used it twice, once inside the numerator and once in evaluating the conjugate product below.

    2. One number for a circuit element . Application, 16 points. Question 2 of 5.

    Application 16 pts

    An electrical engineer records a circuit element by a single complex number, its impedance Z=R+XiZ = R + XiZ=R+Xi measured in ohms, where the real number RRR is resistance and the real number XXX is reactance. Three modelling rules do all the work below. Elements in series have impedances that add. Elements in parallel combine by 1Z=1Z1+1Z2\dfrac{1}{Z} = \dfrac{1}{Z_1} + \dfrac{1}{Z_2}Z1​=Z1​1​+Z2​1​. And voltage, current and impedance are tied together by V=IZV = IZV=IZ, with VVV in volts and III in amperes, both complex.

    1. A
      Part A.

      An element of impedance 5+3i5 + 3i5+3i ohms is placed in series with one of impedance 1−5i1 - 5i1−5i ohms. Find the impedance of the pair, and then the voltage across the pair when the current through it is 2+4i2 + 4i2+4i amperes.

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 4

      Everything here is ordinary complex arithmetic wearing an engineering coat. Read the three modelling rules as arithmetic instructions, and keep the units attached to every line you write.

    2. Hint 2 of 4 · Part B

      A real quantity divided by a complex one is still a division. Multiply above and below by the conjugate of the denominator and look hard at what that denominator turns into before dividing anything.

    3. Hint 3 of 4 · Part C

      The rule asks for two reciprocals, and the lesson gives a formula for one. Build them both, and before inverting the sum, look at how the two numerators are related to each other.

    4. Hint 4 of 4 · Part D

      Multiply a real number by R+XiR + XiR+Xi and ask which slot each piece lands in. Then ask what would have to happen to a product of two nonzero real numbers for the imaginary slot to come out empty.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    6−2i6 - 2i6−2i ohms, and a voltage of 20+20i20 + 20i20+20i volts.

    Part B

    5−i5 - i5−i amperes.

    • 5+(−1)i5 + (-1)i5+(−1)i names the same current; the sign belongs to the imaginary part
    • 5−1i5 - 1i5−1i is the same number, though the coefficient 111 is normally left unwritten

    Part C

    555 ohms; in letters, for a≠0a \neq 0a=0, the combination is a2+b22a\dfrac{a^2 + b^2}{2a}2aa2+b2​ ohms, which is always a real number, and is positive exactly when aaa is positive.

    • a2+b22a\dfrac{a}{2} + \dfrac{b^2}{2a}2a​+2ab2​ is the same expression with the fraction split into two terms

    Part D

    It cannot. With III real and nonzero and Z=R+XiZ = R + XiZ=R+Xi with X≠0X \neq 0X=0, the product is V=IR+IX iV = IR + IX\,iV=IR+IXi, whose imaginary part IXIXIX is a product of two nonzero reals and so is nonzero. When X=0X = 0X=0 the rule reads V=IRV = IRV=IR, so the familiar real-number rule is the special case the complex model contains rather than replaces.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Series impedances add, which is a collection of like terms and nothing more:

    Z=(5+3i)+(1−5i)=(5+1)+(3−5) i=6−2i ohms.Z = (5 + 3i) + (1 - 5i) = (5 + 1) + (3 - 5)\,i = 6 - 2i \ \text{ohms}.Z=(5+3i)+(1−5i)=(5+1)+(3−5)i=6−2i ohms.

    Notice what the two parts did separately. The resistances added to 666, and the reactances, one positive and one negative, partly cancelled to −2-2−2. Recording the element as one complex number is what lets a single addition carry both facts.

    Now apply V=IZV = IZV=IZ, which is an ordinary complex multiplication:

    V=(2+4i)(6−2i)=12−4i+24i−8i2.V = (2 + 4i)(6 - 2i) = 12 - 4i + 24i - 8i^2.V=(2+4i)(6−2i)=12−4i+24i−8i2.

    The last term is the only place the definition of iii is needed, and it turns −8i2-8i^2−8i2 into +8+8+8:

    V=(12+8)+(−4+24) i=20+20i volts.V = (12 + 8) + (-4 + 24)\,i = 20 + 20i \ \text{volts}.V=(12+8)+(−4+24)i=20+20i volts.

    Both answers carry units, and both are complex numbers rather than a pair of unrelated readings.

    Part B

    The rule V=IZV = IZV=IZ is solved for III by dividing, which is legal because the impedance is not 000:

    I=VZ=265+i.I = \frac{V}{Z} = \frac{26}{5 + i}.I=ZV​=5+i26​.

    Clear the complex denominator by multiplying above and below by its conjugate 5−i5 - i5−i. The new denominator is a conjugate product, so it is the real number 52+12=265^2 + 1^2 = 2652+12=26:

    I=26(5−i)(5+i)(5−i)=26(5−i)26=5−i amperes.I = \frac{26(5 - i)}{(5 + i)(5 - i)} = \frac{26(5 - i)}{26} = 5 - i \ \text{amperes}.I=(5+i)(5−i)26(5−i)​=2626(5−i)​=5−i amperes.

    Check it against the model, since one multiplication settles the matter:

    (5−i)(5+i)=25+5i−5i−i2=26.✓(5 - i)(5 + i) = 25 + 5i - 5i - i^2 = 26. \checkmark(5−i)(5+i)=25+5i−5i−i2=26.✓

    Read the answer before leaving it. The voltage was a real number, and the current is not: it has an imaginary part of −1-1−1 ampere. So a real reading on one quantity does not make the other real, which is the point part D takes up in general.

    Part C

    The parallel rule asks for two reciprocals, so build each one with the conjugate trick. For the first element the conjugate product is 22+42=202^2 + 4^2 = 2022+42=20:

    12+4i=2−4i20,12−4i=2+4i20.\frac{1}{2 + 4i} = \frac{2 - 4i}{20}, \qquad \frac{1}{2 - 4i} = \frac{2 + 4i}{20}.2+4i1​=202−4i​,2−4i1​=202+4i​.

    The two reciprocals are themselves conjugates, so adding them cancels the imaginary parts and leaves a real number:

    1Z=2−4i20+2+4i20=420=15,\frac{1}{Z} = \frac{2 - 4i}{20} + \frac{2 + 4i}{20} = \frac{4}{20} = \frac{1}{5},Z1​=202−4i​+202+4i​=204​=51​,

    and therefore Z=5Z = 5Z=5 ohms. The combination behaves as a plain resistance, even though neither element does.

    Now the same computation in letters. With aaa and bbb real and a+bi≠0a + bi \neq 0a+bi=0, the conjugate product is a2+b2a^2 + b^2a2+b2, so

    1a+bi+1a−bi=a−bia2+b2+a+bia2+b2=2aa2+b2.\frac{1}{a + bi} + \frac{1}{a - bi} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2} + \frac{a + bi}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{2a}{a^2 + b^2}.a+bi1​+a−bi1​=a2+b2a−bi​+a2+b2a+bi​=a2+b22a​.

    The two imaginary parts are opposites and cancel exactly, which is the same cancellation the numbers showed. Inverting, and using a≠0a \neq 0a=0,

    Z=a2+b22a.Z = \frac{a^2 + b^2}{2a}.Z=2aa2+b2​.

    Both a2+b2a^2 + b^2a2+b2 and 2a2a2a are real, so the quotient is real for every conjugate pair with a≠0a \neq 0a=0, with no reactance at all. The restriction is not decoration: if aaa were 000 the two reciprocals would be −ib-\frac{i}{b}−bi​ and ib\frac{i}{b}bi​, which cancel to 000, and 1Z=0\frac{1}{Z} = 0Z1​=0 is satisfied by no impedance at all. It is positive exactly when aaa is positive, since a2+b2a^2 + b^2a2+b2 is positive for any a+bia + bia+bi other than 000. Checking the numbers against the letters, a=2a = 2a=2 and b=4b = 4b=4 give 4+164=5\frac{4 + 16}{4} = 544+16​=5, as computed.

    Part D

    Argue from the multiplication itself rather than from examples, since the claim is about every such element.

    Let the current be a real number I≠0I \neq 0I=0 and let the impedance be Z=R+XiZ = R + XiZ=R+Xi with RRR and XXX real and X≠0X \neq 0X=0. Multiplying a complex number by a real number multiplies both parts:

    V=I(R+Xi)=IR+IX i.V = I(R + Xi) = IR + IX\,i.V=I(R+Xi)=IR+IXi.

    Both IRIRIR and IXIXIX are real, so this is already in standard form and its imaginary part can be read off: it is IXIXIX. A product of two nonzero real numbers is nonzero, so IX≠0IX \neq 0IX=0, and a complex number with nonzero imaginary part is not real. The voltage therefore cannot be a real number, whatever the resistance happens to be.

    Notice which fact did the work. It was not anything about iii; it was that the real numbers have no zero divisors, so two nonzero real factors cannot multiply to 000. The imaginary part had no way of vanishing.

    Now set X=0X = 0X=0. The impedance is the real number RRR, and the rule collapses to

    V=IR,V = IR,V=IR,

    which is the rule for a purely resistive element, in which voltage and current are both real and simply proportional. So the complex model does not overturn the older one: it contains it as the case X=0X = 0X=0. That is the pattern worth carrying away from the whole lesson. Enlarging the number system left every law of arithmetic exactly where it was, and only added cases that the old system had no way to describe.

    In one line

    The series pair has impedance 6−2i6 - 2i6−2i ohms and carries a voltage of 20+20i20 + 20i20+20i volts. The element of impedance 5+i5 + i5+i ohms carries a current of 5−i5 - i5−i amperes. The parallel conjugate pair combines to 555 ohms, and in letters to a2+b22a\dfrac{a^2 + b^2}{2a}2aa2+b2​ ohms, which is real for every conjugate pair with a≠0a \neq 0a=0 and positive exactly when aaa is positive. Finally, a real nonzero current through an element with nonzero reactance XXX gives V=IR+IX iV = IR + IX\,iV=IR+IXi with IX≠0IX \neq 0IX=0, so the voltage cannot be real; and when X=0X = 0X=0 the rule becomes V=IRV = IRV=IR, the familiar real-number rule sitting inside the complex one as a special case.

    Reasoning 13 pts

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    The rule holds. Naming q=zwq = \dfrac{z}{w}q=wz​ turns the claim into a statement about the product qw=zqw = zqw=z, and conjugating that gives q‾ w‾=z‾\overline{q}\,\overline{w} = \overline{z}q​w=z; the division by w‾\overline{w}w is legal because w≠0w \neq 0w=0 forces w‾≠0\overline{w} \neq 0w=0.

    Part B

    −75−115 i-\dfrac{7}{5} - \dfrac{11}{5}\,i−57​−511​i by either route.

    • −1.4−2.2i-1.4 - 2.2i−1.4−2.2i is the same number written with decimals

    Exactly the nonzero real and nonzero pure imaginary zzz, that is, the z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi with z≠0z \neq 0z=0 and ab=0ab = 0ab=0. The quotient is 111 for real zzz and −1-1−1 for pure imaginary zzz, so it is never any other real number.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The obstacle is that division is not one of the operations the rule was proved for, so the proof has to turn the quotient into a product first.

    Give the quotient a name. Let

    q=zw,q = \frac{z}{w},q=wz​,

    which exists because w≠0w \neq 0w=0. By what division MEANS, qqq is the number satisfying

    qw=z.qw = z.qw=z.

    That is an equation between two complex numbers, and equal numbers have equal conjugates, so conjugate both sides. The left side is a product, and the product rule proved in the lesson applies to it:

    q‾ w‾=z‾.\overline{q}\,\overline{w} = \overline{z}.q​w=z.

    One step remains, and it is the one that needs justifying: divide both sides by w‾\overline{w}w. That is only allowed if w‾≠0\overline{w} \neq 0w=0. Suppose w‾\overline{w}w were 000. Then the product w w‾w\,\overline{w}ww would be 000 as well, but the lesson computed that product for w=c+diw = c + diw=c+di:

    w w‾=c2+d2,w\,\overline{w} = c^2 + d^2,ww=c2+d2,

    which is 000 only when w=0w = 0w=0, contrary to hypothesis. So w‾≠0\overline{w} \neq 0w=0, the division is legal, and

    q‾=z‾w‾.\overline{q} = \frac{\overline{z}}{\overline{w}}.q​=wz​.

    Since q‾\overline{q}q​ is exactly the left side of the claim, the proof is finished. It is worth seeing why this counts as a proof about DIVISION while dividing nothing until the last step: division was defined in terms of multiplication, so a rule about products reaches quotients automatically, once the quotient is renamed as the solution of a multiplication.

    Part B

    Run the two routes independently and compare only at the end. A shortcut that borrows a line from one route destroys the evidence the other was meant to supply.

    Divide first. Multiply above and below by 1+2i1 + 2i1+2i, the conjugate of the denominator, whose conjugate product is 12+22=51^2 + 2^2 = 512+22=5:

    3+5i1−2i=(3+5i)(1+2i)5=3+6i+5i+10i25.\frac{3 + 5i}{1 - 2i} = \frac{(3 + 5i)(1 + 2i)}{5} = \frac{3 + 6i + 5i + 10i^2}{5}.1−2i3+5i​=5(3+5i)(1+2i)​=53+6i+5i+10i2​.

    Spending 10i2=−1010i^2 = -1010i2=−10 and collecting gives

    −7+11i5=−75+115 i,\frac{-7 + 11i}{5} = -\frac{7}{5} + \frac{11}{5}\,i,5−7+11i​=−57​+511​i,

    and conjugating that flips the sign of its imaginary part alone:

    −75−115 i.-\frac{7}{5} - \frac{11}{5}\,i.−57​−511​i.

    Conjugate first. The two conjugates are 3−5i3 - 5i3−5i and 1+2i1 + 2i1+2i, so the quotient to compute is 3−5i1+2i\frac{3 - 5i}{1 + 2i}1+2i3−5i​. Its denominator is cleared by 1−2i1 - 2i1−2i, and the conjugate product is again 555:

    3−5i1+2i=(3−5i)(1−2i)5=3−6i−5i+10i25.\frac{3 - 5i}{1 + 2i} = \frac{(3 - 5i)(1 - 2i)}{5} = \frac{3 - 6i - 5i + 10i^2}{5}.1+2i3−5i​=5(3−5i)(1−2i)​=53−6i−5i+10i2​.

    Again 10i2=−1010i^2 = -1010i2=−10, so this collects to

    −7−11i5=−75−115 i.\frac{-7 - 11i}{5} = -\frac{7}{5} - \frac{11}{5}\,i.5−7−11i​=−57​−511​i.

    The two routes agree, as part A said they must. Look at where the agreement came from: the two middle terms carry opposite signs in the two numerators, and everything else is untouched, so the two numerators are conjugates of each other while the denominator, being real, is its own conjugate.

    Part C

    Turn the word "real" into an equation, which is what the test is for.

    Write u=zz‾u = \frac{z}{\overline{z}}u=zz​, legal since z≠0z \neq 0z=0. The test says uuu is real exactly when u‾=u\overline{u} = uu=u. Conjugate uuu with the quotient rule from part A, remembering that conjugating twice returns the original number:

    u‾=z‾z‾‾=z‾z.\overline{u} = \frac{\overline{z}}{\overline{\overline{z}}} = \frac{\overline{z}}{z}.u=zz​=zz​.

    So the condition to solve is

    zz‾=z‾z.\frac{z}{\overline{z}} = \frac{\overline{z}}{z}.zz​=zz​.

    Both denominators are nonzero, so multiplying across is legal and the condition becomes z2=z‾2z^2 = \overline{z}^2z2=z2, that is, z2−z‾2=0z^2 - \overline{z}^2 = 0z2−z2=0. Now write z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi with aaa and bbb real and compute the two squares:

    z2=a2−b2+2ab i,z‾2=a2−b2−2ab i.z^2 = a^2 - b^2 + 2ab\,i, \qquad \overline{z}^2 = a^2 - b^2 - 2ab\,i.z2=a2−b2+2abi,z2=a2−b2−2abi.

    Subtracting, the real parts cancel and the imaginary parts add:

    z2−z‾2=4ab i.z^2 - \overline{z}^2 = 4ab\,i.z2−z2=4abi.

    A complex number is 000 exactly when both of its parts are 000, so the condition is 4ab=04ab = 04ab=0, that is, ab=0ab = 0ab=0. Since aaa and bbb are real, this says a=0a = 0a=0 or b=0b = 0b=0: the number is pure imaginary or real. (It cannot be both, since z≠0z \neq 0z=0.)

    Check both cases, which also settles the converse direction and supplies the values. If b=0b = 0b=0 then zzz is a nonzero real and z‾=z\overline{z} = zz=z, so

    zz‾=1.\frac{z}{\overline{z}} = 1.zz​=1.

    If a=0a = 0a=0 then z=biz = biz=bi with b≠0b \neq 0b=0, so z‾=−bi\overline{z} = -biz=−bi and

    zz‾=bi−bi=−1.\frac{z}{\overline{z}} = \frac{bi}{-bi} = -1.zz​=−bibi​=−1.

    Both values are real, so every number allowed by the condition really does work, and the description is exact in both directions. The quotient is never any real number other than 111 or −1-1−1, which is more than was asked and worth noticing: when this quotient is real, conjugation has either left zzz alone or flipped its sign, with nothing in between. For every other zzz the quotient is not real at all, as the retry problem shows.

    In one line

    Conjugation does pass through division: naming q=z/wq = z / wq=z/w gives qw=zqw = zqw=z, conjugating gives q‾ w‾=z‾\overline{q}\,\overline{w} = \overline{z}q​w=z by the product rule, and dividing by w‾\overline{w}w, which is nonzero whenever w≠0w \neq 0w=0 because w w‾=c2+d2w\,\overline{w} = c^2 + d^2ww=c2+d2 is then nonzero, yields q‾=z‾/w‾\overline{q} = \overline{z} / \overline{w}q​=z/w. Both routes to (3+5i1−2i)‾\overline{\left(\frac{3 + 5i}{1 - 2i}\right)}(1−2i3+5i​)​ give −75−115i-\frac{7}{5} - \frac{11}{5}i−57​−511​i. And for z=a+bi≠0z = a + bi \neq 0z=a+bi=0, the quotient zz‾\frac{z}{\overline{z}}zz​ is real exactly when ab=0ab = 0ab=0, that is, exactly for the nonzero real and nonzero pure imaginary zzz, the quotient being 111 in the first case and −1-1−1 in the second.

    Another way: Verify part A by brute force, and see what the structural proof saves

    The rule can also be checked by writing both sides in standard form. With z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi and w=c+diw = c + diw=c+di, the left side needs the quotient computed first:

    zw=(a+bi)(c−di)c2+d2=(ac+bd)+(bc−ad) ic2+d2,\frac{z}{w} = \frac{(a + bi)(c - di)}{c^2 + d^2} = \frac{(ac + bd) + (bc - ad)\,i}{c^2 + d^2},wz​=c2+d2(a+bi)(c−di)​=c2+d2(ac+bd)+(bc−ad)i​,

    so conjugating it flips one sign and gives (ac+bd)−(bc−ad)ic2+d2\frac{(ac + bd) - (bc - ad)i}{c^2 + d^2}c2+d2(ac+bd)−(bc−ad)i​. The right side is a−bic−di\frac{a - bi}{c - di}c−dia−bi​, and clearing ITS denominator with c+dic + dic+di gives (ac+bd)−(bc−ad)ic2+d2\frac{(ac + bd) - (bc - ad)i}{c^2 + d^2}c2+d2(ac+bd)−(bc−ad)i​ as well. The two agree, so the rule is confirmed.

    What this route costs is not generality. With aaa, bbb, ccc and ddd arbitrary it proves exactly the same theorem, and that theorem can then be reapplied wherever it is wanted. What it costs is a page of algebra, and the insight: the structural proof shows WHY the rule holds, namely that division was defined in terms of multiplication, so a rule about products reaches quotients with no separate argument. The coordinate route establishes the same fact while leaving that reason invisible.

    When it is worth it When you distrust a structural argument and want to see the machinery, or when you want the standard form of a conjugated quotient in letters for some later use.

      Reading solutions off a factored equation is a habit worth examining rather than trusting. It is a theorem, its subject is the number zero, and over the complex numbers its proof needs the one thing that the division section supplies.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    Multiplying both sides of zw=0zw = 0zw=0 by the reciprocal 1z\dfrac{1}{z}z1​, which exists because z≠0z \neq 0z=0, and regrouping the left side by associativity, gives 1⋅w=01 \cdot w = 01⋅w=0, so w=0w = 0w=0.

    Part B

    z=2+3iz = 2 + 3iz=2+3i and z=−7z = -7z=−7.

    • The two solutions may be given in either order
    • −7-7−7 may be written −7+0i-7 + 0i−7+0i; it is a real number and also a complex one

    Part C

    It is not sound. Part A is about 000 alone: a product is 000 only if a factor is, and no such statement holds for 555, which has many factorizations. The case z+7=5z + 7 = 5z+7=5 gives z=−2z = -2z=−2, and the product then comes out −95−40i-95 - 40i−95−40i, not 555.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The claim is that the complex numbers have no way for two nonzero factors to multiply to zero. Everything needed is in the division section of the lesson.

    Write z=a+biz = a + biz=a+bi with aaa and bbb real. Since z≠0z \neq 0z=0, the two parts are not both zero, so a2+b2>0a^2 + b^2 > 0a2+b2>0 and the reciprocal exists:

    1z=a−bia2+b2.\frac{1}{z} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2}.z1​=a2+b2a−bi​.

    That formula is available only because a2+b2a^2 + b^2a2+b2 is a nonzero REAL number, which is the conjugate-product theorem doing its work again.

    Now multiply both sides of the hypothesis zw=0zw = 0zw=0 by this number. Multiplying equal numbers by the same number keeps them equal, and anything times 000 is 000, so

    1z(zw)=1z⋅0=0.\frac{1}{z}(zw) = \frac{1}{z} \cdot 0 = 0.z1​(zw)=z1​⋅0=0.

    Regroup the left side. Multiplication of complex numbers is associative, exactly as for real numbers, since it inherits that law along with the others:

    1z(zw)=(1z⋅z)w=1⋅w=w.\frac{1}{z}(zw) = \left(\frac{1}{z} \cdot z\right)w = 1 \cdot w = w.z1​(zw)=(z1​⋅z)w=1⋅w=w.

    Putting the two lines together gives w=0w = 0w=0, which is the claim.

    Two remarks are worth making. First, the hypothesis z≠0z \neq 0z=0 was used exactly once, to know that the reciprocal exists at all, and the proof collapses without it. Second, the argument used no property of iii beyond what makes the reciprocal formula legal, so the same proof would run in any system where every nonzero element has a reciprocal.

    Part B

    Part A licenses the usual reading: a product of complex numbers is 000 only when one of the factors is 000. So the equation splits into two cases, and every solution of the original is a solution of one of them.

    Case 1: the second factor is zero. Then z+7=0z + 7 = 0z+7=0, so z=−7z = -7z=−7.

    Case 2: the first factor is zero. Then

    (4−i)z=11+10i,(4 - i)z = 11 + 10i,(4−i)z=11+10i,

    and since 4−i≠04 - i \neq 04−i=0 it may be divided out. Multiply above and below by the conjugate 4+i4 + i4+i, whose conjugate product with 4−i4 - i4−i is 42+12=174^2 + 1^2 = 1742+12=17:

    z=11+10i4−i=(11+10i)(4+i)17=44+11i+40i+10i217.z = \frac{11 + 10i}{4 - i} = \frac{(11 + 10i)(4 + i)}{17} = \frac{44 + 11i + 40i + 10i^2}{17}.z=4−i11+10i​=17(11+10i)(4+i)​=1744+11i+40i+10i2​.

    Spending 10i2=−1010i^2 = -1010i2=−10 leaves 34+51i17\frac{34 + 51i}{17}1734+51i​, and dividing each part by 171717 gives

    z=2+3i.z = 2 + 3i.z=2+3i.

    Check it in the factor it came from, since one multiplication settles it:

    (4−i)(2+3i)=8+12i−2i−3i2=11+10i,(4 - i)(2 + 3i) = 8 + 12i - 2i - 3i^2 = 11 + 10i,(4−i)(2+3i)=8+12i−2i−3i2=11+10i,

    so the first factor really is 11+10i−11−10i=011 + 10i - 11 - 10i = 011+10i−11−10i=0.

    The two solutions are therefore z=2+3iz = 2 + 3iz=2+3i, from the factor that needed a division, and z=−7z = -7z=−7, from the factor that did not. Nothing in the method changed when the numbers stopped being real; only the arithmetic inside case 2 was new.

    Part C

    Test the method before arguing about it, because a single substitution settles whether it can be trusted.

    The second case gives z+7=5z + 7 = 5z+7=5, so z=−2z = -2z=−2. Put that into the original left side. The first factor is

    (4−i)(−2)−11−10i=−8+2i−11−10i=−19−8i,(4 - i)(-2) - 11 - 10i = -8 + 2i - 11 - 10i = -19 - 8i,(4−i)(−2)−11−10i=−8+2i−11−10i=−19−8i,

    and the second factor is −2+7=5-2 + 7 = 5−2+7=5. Their product is

    (−19−8i)(5)=−95−40i,(-19 - 8i)(5) = -95 - 40i,(−19−8i)(5)=−95−40i,

    which is not 555. So the method produced a number that does not satisfy the equation, and the reasoning cannot be sound.

    Now the reason. Part A established a property of ZERO and of nothing else: if a product is 000, some factor is 000. The step the student copied depends on that property completely. For the number 555 the corresponding claim is simply false, because 555 has endless factorizations over the complex numbers, among them

    5=1⋅5=2⋅52=(1+2i)(1−2i),5 = 1 \cdot 5 = 2 \cdot \tfrac{5}{2} = (1 + 2i)(1 - 2i),5=1⋅5=2⋅25​=(1+2i)(1−2i),

    and a product equals 555 whenever the two factors form ANY of those pairs. Requiring one factor to be 555 picks out a few of the possibilities and rejects the rest, so it neither finds all the solutions nor guarantees that what it finds is a solution at all.

    What should be done instead is to expand the left side, move the 555 across so that one side is 000, and only then look for a factorization. That restores the hypothesis part A needs, which is the general principle: the factored reading is available exactly when the other side is 000, whatever the factors happen to be.

    In one line

    If zw=0zw = 0zw=0 and z≠0z \neq 0z=0, then multiplying by the reciprocal 1z=a−bia2+b2\frac{1}{z} = \frac{a - bi}{a^2 + b^2}z1​=a2+b2a−bi​, which exists because a2+b2≠0a^2 + b^2 \neq 0a2+b2=0, and regrouping by associativity gives w=0w = 0w=0. So ((4−i)z−11−10i)(z+7)=0\bigl((4 - i)z - 11 - 10i\bigr)(z + 7) = 0((4−i)z−11−10i)(z+7)=0 has exactly the solutions z=2+3iz = 2 + 3iz=2+3i and z=−7z = -7z=−7. The same split applied to a right side of 555 is unsound: it produces z=−2z = -2z=−2, for which the product is −95−40i-95 - 40i−95−40i, because the theorem is about 000 alone and 555 has many factorizations.

  5. 5

    5. An unknown and its conjugate at the same time . Application, 14 points. Question 5 of 5.

    Application 14 pts

    An equation can contain a complex unknown and its conjugate together. It looks linear, and the usual first move is to collect the two terms into one. Part-by-part equality is what makes such an equation tractable, and it also decides exactly when the equation is solvable at all.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find every complex number zzz satisfying 2z+3z‾=10−4i2z + 3\overline{z} = 10 - 4i2z+3z=10−4i.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Some students collect the left side of that equation into 5z5z5z and divide by 555. State the assumption about zzz that the collection makes, say for which complex numbers that assumption is true, and decide whether any number satisfying it can solve this equation.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Take the general case. Let ppp and qqq be real numbers, not both zero, let ccc be a complex number, and consider pz+qz‾=cpz + q\overline{z} = cpz+qz=c. Prove that the equation has exactly one solution whenever p2≠q2p^2 \neq q^2p2=q2. Then describe what happens when p=qp = qp=q and when p=−qp = -qp=−q, saying in each case which numbers ccc leave the equation solvable and how many solutions there are.

      Complete the derivation Each line should follow from the one above it. Say what lets you take each step. 6 points

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 3

      An equation containing both zzz and z‾\overline{z}z is not a linear equation in one unknown, however much it resembles one. Write the unknown as x+yix + yix+yi and let the two slots pull the equation into two.

      After the split you have two independent real equations, each of the form (coefficient) times (unknown) equals (constant). Everything turns on when a coefficient can be zero, so factor the hypothesis and see which coefficients it is really talking about.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    z=2+4iz = 2 + 4iz=2+4i, and it is the only solution.

    • Reporting x=2x = 2x=2 and y=4y = 4y=4 is the same answer, provided they are assembled into the single number z=2+4iz = 2 + 4iz=2+4i

    Part B

    Collecting 2z+3z‾2z + 3\overline{z}2z+3z into 5z5z5z assumes z‾=z\overline{z} = zz=z, which is true exactly for real zzz. No real zzz can solve the equation, since for real zzz the left side 5z5z5z is real while the right side has imaginary part −4-4−4.

    Part C

    With z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi and c=u+vic = u + vic=u+vi the split is (p+q)x=u(p + q)x = u(p+q)x=u and (p−q)y=v(p - q)y = v(p−q)y=v. If p2≠q2p^2 \neq q^2p2=q2 both coefficients are nonzero, so zzz is unique. If p=q≠0p = q \neq 0p=q=0 there is a solution only for real ccc; if p=−q≠0p = -q \neq 0p=−q=0, only for ccc with real part 000; in both of those cases there are infinitely many.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Nothing can be collected while zzz and z‾\overline{z}z are both present, so introduce the two real unknowns that describe zzz and let the two slots separate the equation for you.

    Write z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi with xxx and yyy real. Then z‾=x−yi\overline{z} = x - yiz=x−yi, and the left side expands to

    2(x+yi)+3(x−yi)=(2x+3x)+(2y−3y) i=5x−y i.2(x + yi) + 3(x - yi) = (2x + 3x) + (2y - 3y)\,i = 5x - y\,i.2(x+yi)+3(x−yi)=(2x+3x)+(2y−3y)i=5x−yi.

    Both 5x5x5x and −y-y−y are real, so this is in standard form and can be matched against the right side. Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts, so one complex equation becomes two real ones:

    5x=10,−y=−4.5x = 10, \qquad -y = -4.5x=10,−y=−4.

    Each is a one-step equation: x=2x = 2x=2 and y=4y = 4y=4. Assembling them,

    z=2+4i.z = 2 + 4i.z=2+4i.

    Check in the original equation rather than in the derived pair, so that both slots are tested at once:

    2(2+4i)+3(2−4i)=4+8i+6−12i=10−4i.✓2(2 + 4i) + 3(2 - 4i) = 4 + 8i + 6 - 12i = 10 - 4i. \checkmark2(2+4i)+3(2−4i)=4+8i+6−12i=10−4i.✓

    The solution is unique because each of the two real equations determined its unknown outright, leaving no freedom anywhere.

    Part B

    Look at what the collection would have to be using. Adding 2z2z2z and 3z‾3\overline{z}3z into 5z5z5z treats the two terms as multiples of the same number, so it assumes

    z‾=z.\overline{z} = z.z=z.

    That is not a rearrangement, it is an assumption about zzz, and the lesson settles when it holds. If z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi then z‾=z\overline{z} = zz=z says −y=y-y = y−y=y, hence y=0y = 0y=0: the assumption is true exactly for the real numbers, and false for everything else.

    Now test whether the assumption can survive in this problem. Suppose some real number zzz solved the equation. The left side would then genuinely be 5z5z5z, a real number, while the right side 10−4i10 - 4i10−4i has imaginary part −4-4−4, which is not 000. Matching parts, a real number cannot equal a number with nonzero imaginary part, so no real zzz solves it:

    5z=10−4ihas no real solution z.5z = 10 - 4i \quad \text{has no real solution } z.5z=10−4ihas no real solution z.

    So the shortcut is not merely risky here, it is self-defeating. It assumes the unknown is real, and the equation it is applied to has no real solution to find. The distributive law is not what fails: 2z+3z‾2z + 3\overline{z}2z+3z can be collected perfectly well, but only into 2z+3z‾2z + 3\overline{z}2z+3z, since zzz and z‾\overline{z}z are two different numbers unless zzz is real.

    Part C

    Do to the general equation exactly what part A did to the particular one, and then read the answer off the two real equations that result.

    Write z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi and c=u+vic = u + vic=u+vi, with xxx, yyy, uuu, vvv all real. Expanding the left side,

    p(x+yi)+q(x−yi)=(p+q)x+(p−q)y i.p(x + yi) + q(x - yi) = (p + q)x + (p - q)y\,i.p(x+yi)+q(x−yi)=(p+q)x+(p−q)yi.

    Both coefficients are real, so this is standard form and equality of complex numbers applies. One complex equation becomes two real equations that share no unknown:

    (p+q)x=u,(p−q)y=v.(p + q)x = u, \qquad (p - q)y = v.(p+q)x=u,(p−q)y=v.

    That separation is the whole structure of the problem. Each equation has the shape (coefficient) times (unknown) equals (constant), and everything now depends on whether a coefficient is zero.

    The case p2≠q2p^2 \neq q^2p2=q2. Since p2−q2=(p+q)(p−q)p^2 - q^2 = (p + q)(p - q)p2−q2=(p+q)(p−q), the hypothesis says exactly that neither p+qp + qp+q nor p−qp - qp−q is zero. Each real equation may then be divided through, giving

    x=up+q,y=vp−q.x = \frac{u}{p + q}, \qquad y = \frac{v}{p - q}.x=p+qu​,y=p−qv​.

    Both unknowns are forced, so at most one zzz can work; and substituting these values back reproduces ccc, so one does. There is exactly one solution, namely z=up+q+vp−q iz = \frac{u}{p+q} + \frac{v}{p-q}\,iz=p+qu​+p−qv​i.

    The case p=qp = qp=q, with p≠0p \neq 0p=0. The second coefficient is p−q=0p - q = 0p−q=0, so the second equation reads 0⋅y=v0 \cdot y = v0⋅y=v. If v≠0v \neq 0v=0 this is impossible and the equation has no solution at all. If v=0v = 0v=0, which says exactly that ccc is real, then EVERY yyy satisfies it, while the first equation still forces x=u2px = \frac{u}{2p}x=2pu​. So the solutions are all the numbers u2p+yi\frac{u}{2p} + yi2pu​+yi with yyy real: infinitely many.

    The case p=−qp = -qp=−q, with p≠0p \neq 0p=0. Now the first coefficient is p+q=0p + q = 0p+q=0, and the same analysis runs in the other slot. The first equation reads 0⋅x=u0 \cdot x = u0⋅x=u, so there is no solution unless u=0u = 0u=0, which says exactly that the real part of ccc is 000. When u=0u = 0u=0, the second equation forces y=v2py = \frac{v}{2p}y=2pv​ while xxx is free, and again there are infinitely many solutions.

    Collecting the three cases: one solution, none, or infinitely many, which is the same trichotomy a pair of real linear equations always offered. That is the point worth carrying away. Part-by-part equality does not merely help solve this equation, it converts the question into one about a two-by-two real system, and the quantity that decides everything is p2−q2p^2 - q^2p2−q2, the product of the two coefficients the split produced.

    In one line

    2z+3z‾=10−4i2z + 3\overline{z} = 10 - 4i2z+3z=10−4i has the single solution z=2+4iz = 2 + 4iz=2+4i. Collecting the left side into 5z5z5z assumes z‾=z\overline{z} = zz=z, which holds exactly for real zzz, and no real zzz can solve this equation because 5z5z5z would be real while the right side has imaginary part −4-4−4. In general pz+qz‾=cpz + q\overline{z} = cpz+qz=c splits into (p+q)x=u(p + q)x = u(p+q)x=u and (p−q)y=v(p - q)y = v(p−q)y=v: when p2≠q2p^2 \neq q^2p2=q2 both coefficients are nonzero and there is exactly one solution; when p=q≠0p = q \neq 0p=q=0 there is none unless ccc is real, and then infinitely many; when p=−q≠0p = -q \neq 0p=−q=0 there is none unless the real part of ccc is 000, and then infinitely many.

    Another way: Eliminate the conjugate by conjugating the whole equation

    The general equation can also be solved without ever writing z=x+yiz = x + yiz=x+yi. Conjugate both sides of pz+qz‾=cpz + q\overline{z} = cpz+qz=c, using that conjugation passes through sums and products and fixes the real numbers ppp and qqq:

    pz‾+qz=c‾.p\overline{z} + qz = \overline{c}.pz+qz=c.

    Now treat zzz and z‾\overline{z}z as two unknowns in a two-by-two system. Multiplying the original by ppp, the conjugated one by qqq, and subtracting eliminates z‾\overline{z}z:

    (p2−q2)z=pc−qc‾.(p^2 - q^2)z = pc - q\overline{c}.(p2−q2)z=pc−qc.

    When p2≠q2p^2 \neq q^2p2=q2 this gives z=pc−qc‾p2−q2z = \frac{pc - q\overline{c}}{p^2 - q^2}z=p2−q2pc−qc​ directly.

    One step is still owed, and it is easy to skip. The elimination treated zzz and z‾\overline{z}z as two unrelated unknowns, so all it has shown is that no OTHER number could work. To close the argument, conjugate the formula, which is legal because ppp, qqq and p2−q2p^2 - q^2p2−q2 are real and so are their own conjugates:

    z‾=pc‾−qcp2−q2,\overline{z} = \frac{p\overline{c} - qc}{p^2 - q^2},z=p2−q2pc−qc​,

    which is genuinely the conjugate of the first expression, so the pair is consistent rather than two independent guesses. Substituting both into the left side of the original equation,

    pz+qz‾=p(pc−qc‾)+q(pc‾−qc)p2−q2=(p2−q2)cp2−q2=c,pz + q\overline{z} = \frac{p(pc - q\overline{c}) + q(p\overline{c} - qc)}{p^2 - q^2} = \frac{(p^2 - q^2)c}{p^2 - q^2} = c,pz+qz=p2−q2p(pc−qc)+q(pc−qc)​=p2−q2(p2−q2)c​=c,

    since the two terms in c‾\overline{c}c cancel. So the formula really does solve the equation, and not merely rule out every alternative.

    On the numbers of part A, with p=2p = 2p=2, q=3q = 3q=3 and c=10−4ic = 10 - 4ic=10−4i, it gives 2(10−4i)−3(10+4i)−5=−10−20i−5=2+4i\frac{2(10 - 4i) - 3(10 + 4i)}{-5} = \frac{-10 - 20i}{-5} = 2 + 4i−52(10−4i)−3(10+4i)​=−5−10−20i​=2+4i.

    When it is worth it When you want the answer in terms of ccc rather than in terms of its two parts, or when the same equation must be solved for several right-hand sides. It also shows where the condition p2≠q2p^2 \neq q^2p2=q2 comes from, since that is precisely the coefficient the elimination leaves in front of zzz.

    4(2+2i)−(2−2i)=8+8i−2+2i=6+10i.✓4(2 + 2i) - (2 - 2i) = 8 + 8i - 2 + 2i = 6 + 10i. \checkmark4(2+2i)−(2−2i)=8+8i−2+2i=6+10i.✓

    For the second equation, the same expansion gives

    3(x+yi)+3(x−yi)=6x+0⋅y i,3(x + yi) + 3(x - yi) = 6x + 0 \cdot y\,i,3(x+yi)+3(x−yi)=6x+0⋅yi,

    so the imaginary slot of the left side is 000 no matter what zzz is, while the right side has imaginary part 101010. Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts agree, so there is nothing to find.

Marking rubrics

Work every question first. Then mark your own paper against these, giving yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down.

1. Where the new rule actually gets spent 11 points

Part A 5

  • Carries out the sum and the difference by combining like terms, distributing the minus sign through both terms of www in the difference. 2
  • Divides by multiplying above and below by the conjugate of the denominator, and evaluates the new denominator as a real number before dividing anything. 2
  • Reports all four results in the form a+bia + bia+bi, with no power of iii left standing and no single fraction left undivided. 1

Part B 3

  • Produces both expansions in full, with all four partial products written out in each, before comparing anything. 2
  • Names the single term at which the two expansions differ, and says which slot of the answer that term ends up in once the rule is applied. 1

Part C 3

  • Sorts the four operations by the machinery each needs, and names the theorem division depends on together with both things it guarantees about the new denominator. 2
  • Says what form all four results share, and settles whether that shape was forced or was a feature of these particular numbers. 1

2. One number for a circuit element 16 points

Part A 4

  • Adds the two impedances part by part, then multiplies the current by the total, spending i2=−1i^2 = -1i2=−1 where it appears. 2
  • Attaches ohms to the impedance and volts to the voltage. 1
  • Reports both results as single complex numbers in the form a+bia + bia+bi. 1

Part B 3

  • Divides by the impedance using its conjugate, and evaluates the resulting real denominator before dividing either part. 2
  • Reports the current in amperes as one complex number in standard form. 1

Part C 5

  • Writes each reciprocal in standard form using the conjugate, and adds the two before inverting. 2
  • Repeats the computation with aaa and bbb in place of the numbers, reaching a single expression for the combined impedance. 2
  • States what kind of number the combination is for every conjugate pair the question allows, and the condition on aaa under which it is positive. 1

Part D 4

  • Multiplies out the product of a real current with a general impedance and argues from the imaginary slot of the result, rather than testing a single example. 3
  • Says what the rule becomes when the reactance is 000, and what that settles about the relationship between the two rules. 1

3. Conjugation goes through the fourth operation too 13 points

Part A 5

  • Names the quotient, restates the claim as a fact about a product, and applies the product rule for conjugation to that product. 3
  • Justifies that the conjugate of a nonzero number is itself nonzero, before dividing by it. 1

Part B 3

  • Carries out both routes in full, each with its own conjugate multiplication and its own real denominator. 2
  • Reports both results in standard form and states whether they agree. 1

Part C 5

  • Describes every zzz that satisfies the condition and gives the value the quotient takes in each case, so that both directions of the description are covered. 2

4. Reading solutions off a product 14 points

Part A 4

  • Multiplies the hypothesis by the reciprocal of the nonzero factor, and says why that reciprocal exists. 3
  • Names the law that permits regrouping the triple product, rather than performing the regrouping silently. 1

Part A 5
